name: United Kingdom
toneOfVoice: Professional and measured. Slightly more formal than US English, but never stiff. Use plain, direct language and address the reader as 'you'. British spelling and idiom throughout. Avoid Americanisms and overly casual phrasing in policy documents; light warmth is welcome in FAQs and knowledge articles.
contentStrategy: Lead with what the reader needs to know or do, in true BLUF style. UK readers expect competence and brevity; padding undermines trust. Reference local PepsiCo UK operations (Walkers, Quaker UK, Tropicana UK) where contextually relevant. For HR and benefits content, default to plain English with legalese reserved for the citations.
contentGuidelines: 1. Use British spelling consistently (colour, behaviour, organisation, prioritise, programme). 2. Dates as DD/MM/YYYY, currency in GBP with £ prefix. 3. Numeric values: spell out one through nine; use numerals for 10+. 4. Use single quotation marks for the outer pair, double for nested. 5. Reference UK law (UK GDPR, Equality Act 2010, Working Time Regulations) where relevant. 6. Avoid US-specific terms — see terminology below.
regulatoryNotes: Reference UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018 for privacy and data-handling content. For HR content, ground in the Equality Act 2010, Working Time Regulations 1998, and Employment Rights Act 1996. For product-labeling content, reference FSA (Food Standards Agency) guidance and the Natasha's Law allergen requirements. Engage the UK legal team for anything touching on workers' councils or trade-union matters.
seoNotes: UK + EMEA employees expect concise, formal headlines. Use British spelling ("organisation", "colour"). Mention statutory entitlements explicitly (e.g. "statutory sick pay") — these are the exact search terms.
